lines.text: It’s capstone time! Today you run your own mini market stall, using everything you have learned about money.
Pick one simple thing you could make or offer, like bookmarks, greeting cards, lemon water or friendship bands.
It should be cheap to make and something people like.
In class we use play money only.
Cost is the money you spend to make one item.
Price is what the customer pays.
If a bookmark costs ₹6 to make and sells for ₹10, you earn ₹4 on each one.
Profit is the money left after you take away all your costs.
Profit equals the money from sales minus the costs.
If you sell 20 bookmarks for ₹10, you get ₹200, and if they cost ₹120 to make, your profit is ₹80.
A poster shows the product name, the price and one reason to buy.
A sales pitch is one short, friendly sentence you say to customers.
Be honest and never promise what your product cannot do.
Take turns being sellers and buyers with play money.
Give correct change, write every sale in your sales log, and say thank you.
At the end, count your money and work out your profit.
Zoya decides to sell hand-painted bookmarks at the class market.
Each bookmark costs her six rupees to make, and she sells it for ten rupees.
She makes twenty bookmarks, which costs one hundred and twenty rupees.
She sells all twenty for two hundred rupees, so her profit is eighty rupees.
If Zoya sets the price at fifty rupees, it is too high and nobody buys.
If she sets it at five rupees, she loses one rupee on every bookmark, because it costs six to make.
At ten rupees, the price is fair for customers and more than her cost.
A good price is more than your cost, and fair enough that people want to buy.
A great sales pitch starts with a friendly hello and a smile.
Then give one true reason to buy, like each bookmark is hand-painted.
Say the price clearly, so the customer knows exactly what it costs.
And always say thank you, even when someone does not buy.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now plan it, build it, test it, and share it!
